title: The kibbutz
hook: collective farms built on shared work

segments.voice: Yesterday, a language of prayer at the kitchen table, and your line: pass the salt, in Hebrew. Who heard your Hebrew word? Today, a Hebrew word that became a whole way of living. Day one thousand three.

A long dining hall at dusk. Rows of tables, the same plates, the same bread, a hum of people who have worked the same fields since sunrise. Nobody pays at the door. Nobody gets a bill. The person who drove the tractor today might be serving soup tomorrow, and the person serving soup today might be on the tractor. On the wall, a notice for the evening meeting, where everyone gets a vote. This is a kibbutz, and for the young people who built the early ones, this room was the point.
screen: `A LONG DINING HALL.` → `NOBODY GETS A BILL.` → `A MEETING WHERE EVERYONE VOTES.`

segments.voice: Kibbutz is a Hebrew word for a gathering, a group. It shares its root with the word the Torah uses when it promises that God will gather the scattered people back from among the nations. The kibbutz took that old verb and made it a farm. The idea was simple and radical. The members held their property and their earnings in common, not as separate families. They ate together. They shared the work, and jobs often rotated, so nobody was only ever the boss or only ever the dishwasher. Big decisions went to the general meeting, where every member had a voice. Money, clothes, sometimes even the raising of children were arranged in common. The founders of the early ones came out of the labor Zionism of two lessons ago: young people who believed that working the soil with their own hands would heal something in them and in their people. There were also religious kibbutzim, where members shared the work and also kept Shabbat and prayed together. Life was hard: swamps, heat, sickness, arguments. And the kibbutz has changed over the years; some now pay members different salaries and run factories as well as farms. Older members sometimes argue about whether the change was wise. But the picture stays. The psalm puts it in one line, and a song built on it is still sung at Jewish gatherings: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" The psalm calls it good and pleasant. The kibbutz found out it was also work.
screen: `A GATHERING, A GROUP.` · `SHARED WORK, SHARED TABLE.` · `EVERY MEMBER A VOTE.` · `A KIBBUTZ THAT CHANGED.` · then, large: `GOOD AND PLEASANT, AND ALSO WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: share one thing. Settle, and breathe. Run through your day in your mind and find one thing you usually keep for yourself: a meal, a car ride, a skill, an hour, a good book. Nothing grand. Then picture one person who could use it, or simply enjoy it with you. See yourself offering it. Notice whether it feels like losing something or gaining something, or both. Choose the person, and choose the thing. The bell holds the time.
Kibbutz. A gathering, a group: a community that shared its work, its table and its decisions, sometimes secular, sometimes religious. Today's word.
Your line: together. Today, share the one thing you chose, and if you can, share a meal at the same table. Day one thousand three.

howItsDone: Kibbutz members have traditionally shared work, meals and decisions through a general meeting; some kibbutzim are religious and keep Shabbat together, and some have changed their economic arrangements over time.
